questions.prompt: The dual of minimizing \(c^T x\) subject to \(Ax = b\) and \(x \ge 0\) is
options: minimize \(b^T y\) subject to \(A^T y \le c\)
maximize \(b^T y\) subject to \(A^T y \ge c\)
maximize \(b^T y\) subject to \(A^T y \le c\)
questions.explanation: Stationarity of the Lagrangian solves the inequality multiplier as \(s = c - A^T y\). Dual feasibility \(s \ge 0\) is \(A^T y \le c\). After that substitution the Lagrangian equals \(b^T y\), and the dual maximizes it. Minimizing \(b^T y\) runs in the wrong direction. Swapping \(b\) and \(c\), or reversing the inequality, describes a different program.

questions.prompt: Minimize \(-3x\) subject to \(x + s = 7\) with \(x, s \ge 0\). The dual is maximize \(7y\) subject to \(y \le -3\) and \(y \le 0\). What is the optimal dual value?
questions.explanation: The tighter constraint is \(y \le -3\). Maximizing \(7y\) pushes \(y\) up to \(-3\), and the value is \(7 \cdot (-3) = -21\). The primal attains the same number at \(x = 7\), \(s = 0\). Reporting \(21\) drops the sign. Reporting \(-3\) or \(7\) reports the multiplier or the right-hand side. Reporting \(0\) is the dual value at the infeasible-looking but actually feasible point \(y = 0\), which is worse.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: In this standard-form KKT system, the dual slack on column \(j\) is
options: allowed to be negative at a KKT point
questions.explanation: Stationarity rearranges to a nonnegative slack \(s_j = c_j - (A^T y)_j\). That slack is not the primal variable. Complementary slackness ties them together by a product, and they are different numbers. The primal residual \(Ax - b\) is zero at a feasible point. It is not the dual slack. A negative dual slack fails dual feasibility.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that derives the dual of \(\min c^T x\) subject to \(Ax = b\), \(x \ge 0\). Each step uses the previous result.
questions.explanation: The Lagrangian is the object being differentiated, so it comes first. Stationarity produces the slack formula. Dual feasibility is the sign restriction on that slack, and it is the dual constraint. Only after the coefficient of \(x\) has been eliminated does the Lagrangian collapse to \(b^T y\), which the dual maximizes. Maximizing before eliminating \(x\) is not yet a problem in \(y\) alone. Reversing \(s \ge 0\) would produce the opposite dual inequality.

steps: Write the Lagrangian \(c^T x + y^T(b - Ax)\) and introduce a nonnegative multiplier for each \(x_j \ge 0\).
Set the derivative in \(x\) to zero and solve it, obtaining the slack identity \(s = c - A^T y\).
Impose \(s \ge 0\), which is the dual constraint \(A^T y \le c\).
Substitute that stationarity relation back into the Lagrangian to obtain the dual objective \(b^T y\), then maximize it.

questions.prompt: For minimize \(-3x\) subject to \(x + s = 7\), \(x, s \ge 0\), consider the dual multiplier \(y = -3\). Which claims hold?
questions.explanation:
Both dual inequalities hold at \(y = -3\), and \(7 \cdot (-3) = -21\).
• \(y = 0\) is feasible and has objective \(0\), which is worse than \(-21\).
• \(y = -1\) violates \(y \le -3\), so it is not dual feasible.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: A standard-form column with entries \(a\) and \(b\) and cost \(p\) has dual multiplier \((y, z)\). The dual slack of that column equals
questions.explanation: The dual inequality is \(a y + b z \le p\), so the slack that complementary slackness multiplies by the primal variable is \(p - a y - b z\). Every name appears: the two column entries, the two multipliers, and the cost. On the declared ranges the slack is positive. Adding the linear form to \(p\) measures the wrong side of the inequality. Omitting one column entry drops part of \(A^T y\).

questions.prompt: A note derives the dual of \(\min c^T x\) subject to \(Ax = b\), \(x \ge 0\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The equality multiplier is free, and stationarity really does write \(s = c - A^T y\). Substituting a feasible multiplier into the Lagrangian leaves \(b^T y\), which is maximized. The false step reverses the inequality. Nonnegative \(s\) means \(c - A^T y \ge 0\), that is \(A^T y \le c\).

steps: The equality \(Ax = b\) is given a free multiplier \(y\).
Stationarity produces the slack identity \(s = c - A^T y\).
Dual feasibility is the inequality \(A^T y \ge c\).
reasons: Nonnegative slack means \(A^T y \le c\), the opposite inequality.
The equality multiplier should have been nonnegative.

questions.prompt: Minimize \(-6x - 2y\) subject to \(x + y + s = 5\) and \(2x + y + t = 8\), with all four variables nonnegative. What is the optimal value?
questions.explanation: The dual maximizes \(5 y_1 + 8 y_2\) subject to \(y_1 + 2 y_2 \le -6\), \(y_1 + y_2 \le -2\), \(y_1 \le 0\), and \(y_2 \le 0\). The point \(y_1 = 0\), \(y_2 = -3\) is feasible and has value \(-24\). The primal point \(x = 4\), \(y = 0\), \(s = 1\), \(t = 0\) has the same cost, so both are optimal. Reporting \(24\) drops the sign. Reporting \(-12\) is the cost of the feasible but suboptimal point \(x = 2\), \(y = 0\). Reporting \(-3\) is one dual coordinate.

questions.prompt: Weak duality for this standard-form pair says that for every primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible \(y\),
options: the two objectives are equal even when complementary slackness fails
the dual is unbounded whenever the primal is feasible
questions.explanation: A feasible pair cannot put the dual objective above the primal cost. The difference \(c^T x - b^T y\) equals the sum of complementary products, which is nonnegative. Equality needs those products to vanish. It is not automatic. A feasible primal makes the dual bounded above, by that same inequality. It does not make the dual unbounded.

questions.prompt: A proposed primal point has cost \(-18\), and a proposed dual point has value \(-10\). For a minimization primal,
options: the two points cannot both be feasible
questions.explanation: Weak duality requires the dual value to be at most the primal cost. Here \(-10 > -18\), so the inequality is the wrong way around. At least one of the two points is infeasible. Optimality would need a feasible pair with equal values. Neither number alone is a certificate, because the comparison already forbids the pair.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: In the program of minimizing \(-6x - 2y\) subject to \(x + y + s = 5\) and \(2x + y + t = 8\), the point \((x, y, s, t) = (2, 0, 3, 4)\) is primal feasible and \((y_1, y_2) = (0, -3)\) is dual feasible. The duality gap is the primal cost minus the dual objective. What is that gap?
questions.explanation: The primal cost is \(-6 \cdot 2 + (-2) \cdot 0 = -12\). The dual objective is \(5 \cdot 0 + 8 \cdot (-3) = -24\). The gap is \(-12 - (-24) = 12\). Reporting \(-12\) or \(-24\) gives one objective and not the difference. Reporting \(36\) adds the absolute values. The gap is positive, so this primal point is not optimal, even though the dual point happens to be.

questions.prompt: At an optimal standard-form basis, complementary slackness says
options: the equality \(Ax = b\) may be dropped
each positive primal variable has zero dual slack
the equality multipliers must be nonnegative
questions.explanation: The product of each primal variable with its dual slack is zero, so a positive variable forces that slack to vanish. The other dual slacks may be positive. Those belong to primal zeros. The equality \(Ax = b\) is primal feasibility, not something slackness removes. Equality multipliers are free in the Lagrangian. Nonnegativity is for the inequality slacks, not for \(y\).
